questions.text: Explain two reasons why European empire building expanded rapidly in the 19th century.
questions.markScheme: 2 marks per reason (1 for the reason, 1 for a developed explanation or example); accept any two: Economic (Industrial Revolution created demand for raw materials such as cotton, rubber, palm oil and new markets for manufactured goods); Technological (steamships, railways, telegraph, quinine, Maxim gun made conquest and control easier); Political rivalry and nationalism (competition for prestige; Berlin Conference 1884-85 and the Scramble for Africa, by 1914 only Ethiopia and Liberia independent); Ideological and cultural (belief in a 'civilizing mission', missionaries spread Christianity, European languages and education); Strategic (control of trade routes, coaling stations, Suez Canal opened 1869)

questions.context:
Source S4: Extract from Meera's draft investigation (Grade 10 student)
Research question: Is UN peacekeeping good?
Plan: Week 1: Google it. Week 2: write it up.
Sources used: a Wikipedia page on the Rwandan genocide; a 6-minute YouTube video called 'Why the UN Fails'; a blog post by an unnamed author.
Findings: I looked at Rwanda and Srebrenica. In both, peacekeepers did not stop mass killings. This shows UN peacekeeping does not work and the UN should stop doing it.
questions.text: Identify two weaknesses in Meera's research question in Source S4.
questions.markScheme: 1 mark each, max 2: too broad (no place, time or cases defined); 'good' is an undefined value judgement that is not measurable; closed yes/no question; does not name which operations or what counts as success

questions.context:
Source S3: Selected UN peacekeeping operations
UNAMIR | Rwanda, 1993-1996 | 2,500 personnel (cut to about 270 in April 1994) | Failed to prevent the 1994 genocide in which about 800,000 people were killed
UNPROFOR | Former Yugoslavia, 1992-1995 | 39,000 | Could not protect the 'safe area' of Srebrenica, where about 8,000 men and boys were killed in 1995
UNAMSIL | Sierra Leone, 1999-2005 | 17,500 | Disarmed about 75,000 fighters; supported elections in 2002; widely seen as a success
UNTAET | East Timor, 1999-2002 | 11,000 | Ran the territory until independence in 2002
UNIFIL | Southern Lebanon, 1978-present | 10,000 | Has reduced but not ended cross-border fighting
Since 1948 the UN has deployed more than 70 peacekeeping operations.
questions.text: Using Source S3 if helpful, formulate a clear and focused research question about UN peacekeeping, and explain why it is relevant.
questions.markScheme: 2 marks for a clear, focused, open question with defined scope (cases, dates, criterion), 1 if only partly focused; 2 marks for a developed reason it matters, 1 for a simple reason; example question: 'To what extent did the size and mandate of UN peacekeeping operations decide their success in Sierra Leone (1999-2005) and Rwanda (1993-1996)?'; example relevance: the UN still runs about a dozen operations, so knowing why some succeed helps design mandates for current crises and informs debate on the Responsibility to Protect

questions.text: Develop an action plan for a four-week investigation of your research question from Q1(e).
questions.markScheme: Plan is divided into clear weekly stages; Week 1 refines the question and defines success criteria (for example ceasefire held, elections held, no return to war within five years); Week 1 builds a source list; Week 2 collects primary sources (Security Council resolutions, mission reports) and secondary sources (academic studies) with citations; Week 3 analyses each case against the criteria in a comparison table or with an interview or survey; Week 4 drafts, evaluates sources, writes the conclusion, proofreads and completes the bibliography; includes a checkpoint, deadline or contingency (for example a teacher check at end of Week 2); marks by band: 1-2 limited plan with few steps and no timing, 3-4 adequate plan with stages and some timing, 5-6 detailed logical plan with weekly stages, tasks, sources, deadlines and a checkpoint

questions.text: Justify three different methods or sources you would use to collect relevant and varied information for your investigation. Include at least one primary source.
questions.markScheme: Method 1 named and justified (for example UN Security Council resolutions and mission mandates, primary, show what troops were allowed to do); Method 2 named and justified (for example Brahimi Report 2000, an official UN review of peacekeeping failures, or Dallaire's memoir Shake Hands with the Devil, primary eyewitness); Method 3 named and justified (for example academic studies on whether peacekeeping lowers risk of renewed war, secondary with wide sample, or UN data on personnel, budgets and fatalities, quantitative, or an interview with a former peacekeeper, primary but possibly one-sided); the three are varied in type; at least one is primary and its value or limitation is explained

questions.context:
Source S5: Key moments in the Cold War, 1947-1991
1947: Truman Doctrine promises US support to states resisting communism; Marshall Plan aid to Western Europe follows
1949: NATO is formed; the USSR tests its first atomic bomb
1950-1953: Korean War: US-led UN forces fight North Korea and China, which is supplied by the USSR
1955: Warsaw Pact formed by the USSR and Eastern European states
1955-1975: Vietnam War: the USA fights communist North Vietnam, backed by the USSR and China
1957: USSR launches Sputnik, the first artificial satellite
1962: Cuban Missile Crisis brings the superpowers close to nuclear war
1972: SALT I limits some nuclear weapons
1979-1989: Soviet war in Afghanistan; the USA arms Afghan resistance fighters (mujahideen)
1986: Global nuclear stockpile peaks at about 70,000 warheads
1987: INF Treaty removes a whole class of nuclear missiles
1989-1991: Berlin Wall falls (1989); USSR dissolves (1991)
questions.text: Using Source S5, outline how the USA and the USSR competed through the arms race and proxy wars without fighting each other directly.
questions.markScheme: Arms race: both built up nuclear weapons, stockpiles peaking at about 70,000 warheads in 1986, space race (Sputnik 1957) showed missile technology; Deterrence: mutually assured destruction made direct war too dangerous as the Cuban Missile Crisis (1962) showed; Proxy wars: each backed opposite sides in other countries' wars such as Korea (1950-53), Vietnam (1955-75) and Afghanistan (1979-89); Ideology: competition was also to prove capitalism and democracy or communism the better system; max 3 marks, full marks need at least one reference to S5

questions.text: Using Sources S2 and S6, explain one similarity and one difference between the European Union and an empire such as Rome.
questions.markScheme: 1 mark for a valid similarity (both bring many peoples under shared laws and institutions, Roman law and EU law that can override national law; both remove barriers to movement and trade, Roman roads and coinage and the EU single market and euro); 1 mark for a valid difference (EU membership is voluntary and by treaty and members can leave, the UK left in 2020, while Rome expanded by conquest under an emperor; EU decisions are made by elected governments and a Parliament while Roman provinces had no equal say); 1 mark for developing either point with evidence from S2 or S6

Source S7: Resources, trade routes and power (figures approximate)
- About 20 million barrels of oil a day, around one-fifth of world oil consumption, passes through the Strait of Hormuz.
- The Strait of Malacca carries over 20 million barrels of oil a day and a large share of Asia's seaborne trade.
- China processes about 90% of the world's rare earth elements, used in electronics, wind turbines and missiles.
- The Democratic Republic of the Congo mines about 70% of the world's cobalt, used in electric vehicle batteries.
- Russia supplied about 40% of the EU's gas imports in 2021. After the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, this fell to under 20% by 2024.
- Attacks on shipping in the Red Sea in 2023-2024 cut traffic through the Suez Canal by more than half.
questions.text: Write a briefing article (450-600 words) for Youth Model UN delegates aged 13-16 with the title: 'Are empires a thing of the past? Alliances, rivalry and resources in today's world'. In your article, you should: explain why nations form alliances, using at least two organizations from S6; explain how Cold War rivalry (S5) shaped the alliances that exist today; explain how control of resources and trade routes (S7) creates power and economic dependence in a globalized world; reach a clear judgment on whether empire-like power still exists today; use a style, tone and structure suited to your audience and purpose; refer to the sources you use, and include a short source list at the end.
questions.markScheme: Marked for Criterion C: style for audience and purpose max 4, structure max 5, documenting sources max 4; Style 4: consistently clear, engaging and suited to young delegates with terms explained and well chosen examples; Structure 5: logical paragraphs, linking, headings or sub-headings suited to an article, building to a clear judgment; Sources 4: sources consistently acknowledged in the text and a complete consistent source list; Content (inaccurate or irrelevant content limits style to 2): why alliances form is explained, collective security (NATO Article 5), economic gain (EU single market, ASEAN trade), shared identity and values, a voice for emerging economies (BRICS), balancing a rival; Cold War legacy explained, NATO and Warsaw Pact blocs, NATO outlived the USSR and expanded to 32 members, UN Security Council veto reflects 1945 power balance; Resources and dependence explained, chokepoints (Hormuz, Malacca, Suez) give leverage, China's 90% share of rare earth processing and DRC cobalt create dependence, EU reliance on Russian gas before 2022 shows energy used as a weapon, globalization both deters war and creates vulnerability; Judgment supported, formal empires mostly ended through decolonization but empire-like influence continues through military reach, economic dependence, debt, resources and soft power; accept any supported judgment

questions.context:
Source S8: Thomas Babington Macaulay, Minute on Indian Education, 2 February 1835. Macaulay was a British politician serving on the Governor-General's council in India.
'I have never found one among them who could deny that a single shelf of a good European library was worth the whole native literature of India and Arabia... We must at present do our best to form a class who may be interpreters between us and the millions whom we govern; a class of persons, Indian in blood and colour, but English in taste, in opinions, in morals, and in intellect.'

Source S9: Adapted summary of Dadabhai Naoroji, Poverty and Un-British Rule in India, 1901. Naoroji was an Indian economist and politician, and in 1892 became the first Asian elected to the British Parliament.
Britain takes India's wealth out of the country every year through salaries and pensions paid to British officials, interest on debts, and profits sent home. This 'drain' keeps millions of Indians in poverty and famine. Indians are kept out of high office in their own country. Such rule is 'un-British': it betrays the British ideals of justice and fair government that Britain claims to bring.
questions.text: Compare and contrast the perspectives of Source S8 and Source S9 on British rule in India. In your answer, refer to cultural assimilation, resistance, and the impact on Indian identity.
questions.markScheme: Macaulay's perspective described: an imperial official who sees European culture as superior and wants English education to create an anglicized class; cultural assimilation threatens indigenous identity as Indian and Arabic learning is dismissed; Naoroji's perspective described: an Indian nationalist focused on economic exploitation (the 'drain') and exclusion from power; Naoroji's argument is a form of resistance within the British system; a valid similarity or contrast is made with reference to both sources, for example both accept British ideals have value but Naoroji uses them against British rule; insight, for example English-educated Naoroji shows Macaulay's policy producing critics of empire and feeding nationalism (Indian National Congress 1885); band guide 1 one perspective, 2 both described separately, 3 compared with some source reference, 4 clearly compared using both sources and linking assimilation, resistance and identity

questions.context:
Source S11: Description of a cartoon by Will Dyson, published in the British newspaper the Daily Herald, May 1919. Dyson was an Australian cartoonist; the Daily Herald supported the Labour movement.
The four Allied leaders are leaving the Versailles peace conference. French Prime Minister Clemenceau turns his head and says: 'Curious! I seem to hear a child weeping!' Behind a pillar, a small child cries over a document labelled 'Peace Treaty'. Above the child are the words '1940 Class', meaning the young people who would be old enough to be soldiers in 1940. The cartoon is titled 'Peace and Future Cannon Fodder'.
questions.text: With reference to its origin and purpose, evaluate the value and limitations of Source S11 for a historian studying reactions to the Treaty of Versailles.
questions.markScheme: Origin identified, for example a May 1919 cartoon by Will Dyson in the Daily Herald, which supported the Labour movement; Purpose identified, for example to criticise the Allied leaders and persuade readers the treaty would cause another war; Value explained, for example made at the time of the treaty it shows that some in Britain feared another war and the '1940 Class' label was strikingly accurate; Limitation explained, for example it presents one viewpoint from a newspaper critical of the Allied governments, cartoons simplify and exaggerate to persuade, many British and French people in 1919 wanted Germany punished harder, an accurate prediction does not prove the treaty caused the war, and only a description not the image is available; band guide 1-2 identifies origin or purpose and states a value or limitation, 3-4 uses origin and purpose to explain both value and limitation

questions.context:
Source S12: The Treaty of San Francisco with Japan, signed 8 September 1951
Article 14(a): 'It is recognized that Japan should pay reparations to the Allied Powers for the damage and suffering caused by it during the war. Nevertheless it is also recognized that the resources of Japan are not presently sufficient, if it is to maintain a viable economy, to make complete reparation for all such damage and suffering and at the same time meet its other obligations.'
Context: Japan and 48 other nations signed. The treaty ended the US-led occupation in 1952. Japan gave up Korea, Taiwan and other territories. On the same day, Japan signed a security treaty allowing US forces to stay in Japan. The USSR attended but refused to sign. Neither government of China was invited. India declined to attend and signed a separate peace treaty with Japan in 1952.

Source S13: Adapted summary of a speech by John Foster Dulles, chief US negotiator, at the San Francisco conference, 5 September 1951. Dulles had been a young US legal adviser at the 1919 Paris Peace Conference.
This is a treaty of reconciliation, not of vengeance. Past peace settlements have too often planted the seeds of the next war. Japan is restored to equality among nations. We will not impose reparations that would wreck its economy, because a ruined and bitter Japan would threaten the peace of Asia.
questions.text: Using Sources S12 and S13, interpret how the Cold War influenced the peace settlement with Japan.
questions.markScheme: With China communist (1949) and the Korean War under way, the USA wanted Japan as a stable ally so reparations were limited to keep its economy 'viable' (S12); Dulles feared a 'ruined and bitter Japan' (S13) would be unstable and open to communism; the security treaty kept US forces in Japan and the USSR's refusal to sign and China's exclusion show the Cold War division; max 2 if only one source is used

questions.context:
Source S10: The Treaty of Versailles, signed 28 June 1919
Article 231: 'The Allied and Associated Governments affirm and Germany accepts the responsibility of Germany and her allies for causing all the loss and damage to which the Allied and Associated Governments and their nationals have been subjected as a consequence of the war imposed upon them by the aggression of Germany and her allies.'
Other terms: Germany lost about 13% of its European territory and all its colonies; its army was limited to 100,000 men with no air force; reparations were set in 1921 at 132 billion gold marks. Germany was not allowed to negotiate the terms, and many Germans called the treaty a Diktat (dictated peace). The treaty also created the League of Nations.

Source S11: Description of a cartoon by Will Dyson, published in the British newspaper the Daily Herald, May 1919. Dyson was an Australian cartoonist; the Daily Herald supported the Labour movement.
The four Allied leaders are leaving the Versailles peace conference. French Prime Minister Clemenceau turns his head and says: 'Curious! I seem to hear a child weeping!' Behind a pillar, a small child cries over a document labelled 'Peace Treaty'. Above the child are the words '1940 Class', meaning the young people who would be old enough to be soldiers in 1940. The cartoon is titled 'Peace and Future Cannon Fodder'.

Nevertheless it is also recognized that the resources of Japan are not presently sufficient, if it is to maintain a viable economy, to make complete reparation for all such damage and suffering and at the same time meet its other obligations.'
Context: Japan and 48 other nations signed. The treaty ended the US-led occupation in 1952. Japan gave up Korea, Taiwan and other territories. On the same day, Japan signed a security treaty allowing US forces to stay in Japan. The USSR attended but refused to sign. Neither government of China was invited. India declined to attend and signed a separate peace treaty with Japan in 1952.

Source S13: Adapted summary of a speech by John Foster Dulles, chief US negotiator, at the San Francisco conference, 5 September 1951. Dulles had been a young US legal adviser at the 1919 Paris Peace Conference.
This is a treaty of reconciliation, not of vengeance. Past peace settlements have too often planted the seeds of the next war. Japan is restored to equality among nations. We will not impose reparations that would wreck its economy, because a ruined and bitter Japan would threaten the peace of Asia.

Source S14: Adapted from a secondary-school history textbook, 2021
Most historians now argue that the Treaty of Versailles alone did not cause the Second World War. The Great Depression, the weakness of the League of Nations and the policy of appeasement in the 1930s mattered at least as much. Some say the treaty was harsh enough to anger Germans but not harsh enough to stop Germany rising again. Japan after 1951 became a close US ally and one of the world's largest economies. However, disputes over wartime history with China and Korea, and the unresolved Kuril Islands dispute with Russia, show that the 1951 settlement did not resolve every conflict.
questions.text: 'Peace treaties that punish the defeated lead to future wars; peace treaties that rebuild them create lasting peace.' To what extent do you agree with this statement? Answer with reference to the Treaty of Versailles (1919) and the Treaty of San Francisco (1951). In your answer, you should: explain the purpose of peace treaties and the role of diplomacy and negotiation; compare the aims, terms and outcomes of the two treaties; use at least three of the sources S10-S14, including a comment on the origin, purpose, value or limitation of at least one; use your own knowledge, including other causes of the Second World War; consider more than one perspective and reach a supported conclusion.
questions.markScheme: Purpose of treaties and diplomacy explained: end war, settle borders, assign responsibility, prevent new conflict; Versailles was dictated while San Francisco was negotiated over months by Dulles; For the statement: Versailles war guilt clause (S10), reparations of 132 billion gold marks, territorial loss and the Diktat fuelled resentment that Hitler exploited; S11 predicted another war; Ruhr occupation and hyperinflation of 1923 deepened anger; San Francisco limited reparations (S12) and aimed at reconciliation (S13) and Japan became a stable democracy and US ally; Marshall Plan for West Germany shows the same lesson; Against or qualifying: S14 says the Depression, League weakness and appeasement mattered as much; reparations were cut (Dawes 1924, Young 1929) and ended in 1932 so Versailles was not fully enforced; Japan surrendered unconditionally and was occupied and rebuilt before the treaty and US generosity was strategic (Cold War); the 1951 peace is incomplete with no Japan-Russia treaty, the Kuril dispute, history disputes with China and Korea, and China and the USSR excluded; Source evaluation: S13 is from the US negotiator persuading the conference so presents US motives positively; S14 is secondary with hindsight but simplified for students; S11 origin and purpose commented on; Comparison of aims, terms and outcomes of both treaties is explicit; At least three sources used; Judgment supported, for example largely true but treaty terms mattered less than economic conditions and great-power willingness to enforce or support the peace, accept any supported conclusion; Sustained balanced argument with sources integrated and critically evaluated and other causes weighed (band 13-14); Well-supported synthesis with source evaluation and different perspectives (band 10-12); Discusses both treaties with some source use and recognises another view (band 7-9); Some discussion with descriptive source use and one perspective (band 4-6); band 1-3 limited and mainly narrative

questions.context:
Source S15: Factfile on peace, people and global cooperation
- 1930: Mohandas Gandhi leads the Salt March, a non-violent protest against the British salt tax in India. Around 60,000 people are later arrested in the civil disobedience campaign.
- 1995-2002: South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission, chaired by Archbishop Desmond Tutu, takes statements from over 21,000 victims of apartheid-era abuses. Perpetrators could apply for amnesty if they told the full truth.
- 2014: Malala Yousafzai becomes the youngest Nobel Peace Prize winner for her campaign for girls' education.
- Humanitarian organizations: The International Committee of the Red Cross (founded 1863) protects victims of war under the Geneva Conventions. Medecins Sans Frontieres (founded 1971) provides medical aid in conflict zones in over 70 countries.
- 2015: Under the Paris Agreement, almost every country agrees to keep global warming well below 2 degrees C, aiming for 1.5 degrees C.
- 2021-2023: The COVAX initiative delivers nearly 2 billion COVID-19 vaccine doses to 146 countries.
- Terrorism: After the attacks of 11 September 2001, UN Security Council Resolution 1373 requires all states to act against terrorist financing.
- Cyber warfare: In 2017 the NotPetya cyberattack spread from Ukraine across the world, causing an estimated US$10 billion in damage.
- Media: In 1994 the radio station RTLM broadcast hate propaganda that encouraged the genocide in Rwanda. In 2018 a UN fact-finding mission said Facebook had played a 'determining role' in spreading hate against the Rohingya in Myanmar.
questions.text: You have been chosen to give a speech (500-650 words) at a youth assembly for the UN International Day of Peace (21 September). Your audience is students aged 15-18 from many countries. Your title is: 'What will it take to build sustainable peace in the 21st century?' In your speech, you should: explain at least two threats to peace today (for example terrorism and extremism, cyber warfare, or the media's role in shaping perceptions); explain the roles of international organizations, NGOs and individuals in promoting peace; propose at least two long-term peace strategies (for example inclusive societies, education, reconciliation and restorative justice, fair distribution of resources, international cooperation); explain the responsibility of young global citizens; use a style, tone and structure suited to a spoken speech for this audience; acknowledge at least three items from S15 in your speech.
questions.markScheme: Marked for Criterion C: style for audience and purpose max 4, structure max 4, acknowledging sources max 4; Style 4: persuasive and engaging throughout with direct address, rhetorical questions, examples and a call to action for 15-18 year olds; Structure 4: strong hook, logically linked sections and memorable conclusion; Sources 4: at least three items from S15 acknowledged accurately and naturally within the speech; Content (inaccurate or irrelevant content limits style to 2): threats explained, terrorism and extremism (9/11, Resolution 1373), cyber warfare hitting civilians and economies (NotPetya), media and misinformation spreading hate (RTLM in Rwanda, Facebook in Myanmar); roles explained, UN (Security Council, peacekeeping, agencies), NGOs and humanitarian organizations (ICRC, MSF) bring aid and protect civilians, individuals (Gandhi's non-violence, Tutu and Mandela's reconciliation, Malala and education); long-term strategies proposed, inclusive societies and equality, education against prejudice, reconciliation and restorative justice (the TRC), fair distribution of resources, international cooperation (Paris Agreement, COVAX); global citizen responsibility, check information before sharing, challenge hate speech, volunteer, learn about other cultures, take part in civic life
